Your job is to: 1. Determine which documents are needed based on the client's profile 2. Send clear, specific requests via the client's preferred channel 3. Accept uploaded documents and classify them 4. Validate document quality and completeness 5. Track collection status and send follow-ups for missing items 6. Extract key data fields and push to [target system] Rules: - Always be specific about what's needed (not "send financial documents" but "your Chase bank statement for October and November 2026, all pages") - When a document fails quality checks, explain exactly what's wrong and what to re-send - Follow up on missing documents after 48 hours, then every 72 hours - Escalate to a human after 3 failed follow-ups or if the [...] Exception review. When the agent's confidence on a classification is below threshold, a human looks at it. This should be 3–10% of documents for common types, higher for unusual ones.
 Judgment calls. "The client sent a letter from their accountant instead of a formal tax return — does this work?" That's a human decision.
 Frustrated clients. When someone is confused, annoyed, or has a complicated situation, the agent should escalate to a person. Build this escalation trigger into the agent's instructions.
 Final sign-off. The agent assembles and validates the file. A human does the final review and approval. This should take 15–30 minutes instead of 2–3 hours because all the grunt work is done.

results.title: Document Collection Software - Stop Chasing Client Files
results.content:
### Automated Follow-Up Sequences

Set reminder schedules that run without intervention. A few days in: gentle nudge. One week: firmer reminder. Two weeks: escalation. Good software lets you customize timing, tone, and channels (email vs. SMS).

### File Validation

Reject incorrect file types before they're submitted. If you need PDFs, don't accept JPG screenshots of documents. Some tools validate file size, format, and even basic completeness checks.

### Secure Transmission

Encryption at rest and in transit should be standard. Look for password protection, expiration dates, and the ability to restrict downloads. For sensitive documents, audit logs that track who accessed what and when.

### Integration Options [...] ## Why Email-Based Collection Fails

Most professionals still collect documents through email. The process looks familiar: send a list of needed files, wait days for responses, send follow-ups, piece together attachments from multiple threads, and hope nothing gets lost. The numbers tell the story. Manual document collection takes considerable time per client on average. Email-based requests frequently result in submissions needing follow-up because files are missing, mislabeled, or sent to the wrong thread. Staff spend more time organizing and chasing than actually reviewing documents. Common failure points include:

The hidden cost is client experience. Nobody enjoys hunting through their computer for files while wondering if their accountant received the last batch. [...] These files are larger, less standardized, and come from multiple stakeholders. A brand manager sends the guidelines while the legal team handles licensing. The previous agency might have assets the client doesn't even know about. Creative-specific considerations:

## Measuring Collection Efficiency

Track these metrics to see if your new process is working:

### Time to Complete

Measure days from initial request to final submission. Automated collection cuts turnaround time compared to email.

### Follow-Up Rate

What percentage of requests need manual intervention beyond automated reminders? Good software reduces this rate. If you're still manually chasing half your requests, something in the setup needs adjustment.

results.content:
### Faster Turnaround and Reduced Chasing

Manual document requests often feel like endless cycles of reminders, follow-ups, and lost attachments. Automation trims this inefficiency, sending instant requests and timely reminders without anyone lifting a finger. Clients and colleagues respond faster when the process is structured and clear, which pushes projects forward instead of stalling them in inbox limbo.

### Fewer Errors and More Consistency

Collecting dozens, or hundreds, of files through email increases the risk of missing documents, duplicate requests, or version confusion. Automated systems ask for the right files, in the right format, every time. This makes reviews simpler: no more sifting through confusing threads or misfiled attachments.
